content: Surgical intervention continues to be a viable treatment option for tubal infertility, even though the use of in vitro fertilization (IVF) has become increasingly common. The estimated live birth rates following surgery vary significantly, ranging from 9% in women with severe tubal disease to 69% in those with mild disease. However, the effectiveness of surgical treatment has not been rigorously compared to other approaches, such as IVF or expectant management (i.e., no treatment). Furthermore, live birth rates have not been thoroughly evaluated in relation to the severity of tubal damage. It is critical to assess the effectiveness of surgery in comparison to alternative treatments for tubal infertility, given concerns about potential adverse outcomes, intraoperative complications, and the financial costs associated with tubal surgery, as well as the availability of other options like IVF. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of surgical treatment compared to expectant management or IVF in improving live birth rates for women with tubal infertility, regardless of the severity of the condition. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in October 2016 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility (CGF) Group trials register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, Embase, the Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL), and PsycINFO. Additional sources, such as clinical trial registries, unpublished literature, and reference lists of relevant trials and systematic reviews, were also examined. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were deemed eligible for inclusion in this review. The primary outcome of interest was the live birth rate per participant. Secondary outcomes included pregnancy rates and adverse events, such as miscarriage rates, ectopic pregnancy rates, and complications related to the surgical procedure. The review protocol included plans for two independent reviewers to assess trial eligibility, evaluate the risk of bias, and extract data. Data were to be pooled to calculate odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Statistical heterogeneity was to be assessed using the I² statistic, and the overall quality of evidence was to be evaluated using GRADE methodology. However, no suitable randomized controlled trials were identified during the review process. As a result, the relative effectiveness of tubal surgery compared to expectant management and IVF in achieving live births for women with tubal infertility remains unknown. There is a pressing need for large, well-powered trials to determine the efficacy of surgical treatment in this population. Future studies should not only report live birth rates per patient but also compare adverse effects and treatment costs over an extended period. Key factors that significantly influence these outcomes, such as the type of fertility treatment, the age of the female partner, the duration of infertility, and prior pregnancy history, should be carefully considered. Additionally, researchers should report live birth rates in relation to the severity of tubal damage and the specific surgical techniques employed, including microsurgical and laparoscopic methods.
